conclusion: You are a non-secretor: neither of your two copies of FUT2 works. FUT2 makes the blood group sugars - the same sugar tags that decide your ABO blood group - in the cells lining your mouth, gut and other moist surfaces, so it decides whether those sugars appear in saliva and other body fluids. Your red blood cells carry your ABO group as usual, because a different gene puts the sugars there. In you, FUT2 does not work, so these sugars are missing from your body fluids. It is not a disease and there is nothing to treat. About 1 in 5 people of European ancestry are non-secretors: 20% of Swedish blood donors in one study and 25% of the women in a large British one, and the proportion differs in other parts of the world. Compared with secretors, you are largely protected against the most common noroviruses, the winter vomiting bug - that is well established, although the protection is strong rather than absolute, since a non-secretor did fall ill in one outbreak. The trade-off is that a few other conditions are somewhat more common: in that British study 68% of non-secretors reported having had mumps compared with 48% of secretors, and large European studies link being a non-secretor to a somewhat higher chance of type 1 diabetes, which even so remains an uncommon condition. Those are small differences and not destiny. One curiosity: the non-working version was almost absent among Europe's early hunter-gatherers, arrived with the first farmers from Anatolia about 8,000 years ago and then spread, possibly because it protected people in crowded farming settlements from gut viruses. A laboratory can confirm secretor status from saliva; whether that is ever worth doing is for a doctor to decide.

You are a weak secretor: your FUT2 gene works, but only partly. FUT2 makes the blood group sugars - the same sugar tags that decide your ABO blood group - in the cells lining your mouth, gut and other moist surfaces, so it decides whether those sugars appear in saliva and other body fluids; your red blood cells carry your ABO group as usual, because a different gene puts the sugars there. You have either two partly working copies or one partly working copy and one that does not work at all, so less of these sugars reach your body fluids than in most people. It is not a disease, and there is nothing you would notice day to day: the difference shows up in the laboratory, where the partly working version did about a fifth as much of the gene's work as a working one when it was measured in cells. The partly working version is common in East Asia, where about 4 in 10 gene copies carry it and, in one Chinese study of 316 people, about 1 in 6 people had two copies of it; elsewhere it is rare. There is early evidence that it also gives some protection against the gut viruses that non-secretors are protected from, but it has been studied far less than the non-working version, so how much protection it gives is not known. A laboratory can confirm secretor status from saliva if a doctor ever thinks it useful.

You are a secretor: at least one of your two copies of FUT2 works. FUT2 makes the blood group sugars - the same sugar tags that decide your ABO blood group - in the cells lining your mouth, gut and other moist surfaces, so those sugars are present in your body fluids; your red blood cells carry your ABO group as usual, because a different gene puts the sugars there. This is the usual state, and one working copy is enough: in the large studies that have looked, people with one working and one non-working copy release the sugars just as well as people with two working copies, and that holds for norovirus, rotavirus and the conditions studied most closely; a few studies do see small in-between effects for other conditions, such as asthma and arthritis. About 4 in 5 people of European ancestry are secretors, and the proportion differs elsewhere in the world. Compared with a non-secretor, you can catch the common noroviruses - the winter vomiting bug - and rotavirus more easily, because those viruses use these sugars to attach to the gut lining; that is well established for norovirus, and supported by recent work for the common rotavirus strains, and it is an ordinary susceptibility that most secretors never think about. It cuts both ways: non-secretors carry slightly higher chances of a few other conditions, so neither result is the better one. It is not a disease and there is nothing to do about it. If you have ever had a saliva test for secretor status, this is the trait it was reading. This file reads only the two most common non-working versions of FUT2; others, commoner in East Asia, the Pacific and Africa, are not tested, so a secretor result is less certain for people with that ancestry - in one Korean survey a non-working fusion version alone accounted for about 11 in 100 gene copies.

Your DNA file does not show enough of the FUT2 gene to say whether you are a secretor - whether your saliva and other body fluids carry your blood group sugars - so we do not guess. A laboratory can read secretor status directly from a saliva sample if a doctor thinks it is worth knowing.
